baseProblem.statement: Given a sorted array that has been rotated at some unknown pivot, find the index of a target value in O(log n) time. Return -1 if not found.

rounds.question: What state drives a binary search?

options.conceptLabel: Low and high bounds over the whole array
options.rationale: Binary search narrows a [lo, hi] range; start it spanning the entire array.
One index gives a linear O(n) scan, not the O(log n) the problem demands.
Membership tracking is for unsorted search; it ignores the sorted-rotated structure that enables log-time search.

options.conceptLabel: Low, high, and a running best

fragments.java: int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1; int best = -1;

options.rationale: Nothing is being maximized — you return the moment you find target, so an extra accumulator is dead weight.

rounds.question: With lo and hi spanning the array, how does the search loop run?

options.rationale: A full linear pass is O(n) and throws away the log-time advantage.

options.conceptLabel: While the bounds have not crossed
options.rationale: Keep halving while the search range is non-empty; lo <= hi still includes the single-element case.

options.conceptLabel: While lo is strictly less than hi
options.rationale: Stopping at lo < hi skips checking the final single element, so a target sitting there is missed.
An unbounded loop needs an explicit break on an empty range; as written it can spin forever when target is absent.

rounds.question: Inside the loop, what do you compute and check first each step?

options.conceptLabel: Midpoint as the average of the end values
options.rationale: mid must be an INDEX, not an average of values; this indexes nums by a value and breaks.

options.conceptLabel: Midpoint, but compare it to nums[lo]

fragments.java: int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (nums[mid] == nums[lo]) return mid;

options.rationale: You're searching for target, so the hit test is nums[mid] == target, not == nums[lo].

options.conceptLabel: Midpoint index, return if it equals target

fragments.java: int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;

options.rationale: Compute the middle index and short-circuit the moment you land on target.

options.conceptLabel: Midpoint via lo + hi without halving

fragments.java: int mid = lo + hi; if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;

options.rationale: lo + hi runs off the end of the array; the midpoint is (lo + hi) // 2.

rounds.question: When mid isn't the target, which half do you keep, given the array is rotated?

options.conceptLabel: Find the sorted half, then narrow by whether target lies in it
options.rationale: Exactly one side of mid is sorted; if target falls within that sorted side's range, search it, otherwise search the other.
Plain binary search assumes full sorted order; rotation means target may be on either side, so you can't blindly drop one half.

fragments.java: if (nums[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1;

options.rationale: That's the unrotated rule; at the rotation point it sends you the wrong way and misses the target.
Snapping both bounds to mid abandons the rest of the array after a single miss.

rounds.question: If the loop ends, what do you return?

options.rationale: An exhausted range means target isn't present; the contract is -1 in that case.
lo is just where the search stopped, not a valid index of target.
mid holds the last probe, which by definition wasn't target.
The contract is an index (or -1), not a boolean / placeholder.

lightning.question: Why is this O(log n) even though the whole array isn't sorted?
options: Every iteration at least one half is provably sorted, and O(1) bound checks decide if the target is inside it — so half the range is always discarded
The rotation point is located first
It's actually O(n) in the worst case
lightning.explanation: A rotated array split at mid always leaves one side fully sorted. Membership in a sorted range is a two-comparison check, so each step halves the search space — classic O(log n).

lightning.question: Why nums[lo] <= nums[mid] (with equals) instead of strict <? Which input breaks strict comparison?
options: [3, 1] with target 1 — lo == mid there, and strict < would misread the left half as unsorted and search the wrong side
No input — it's a style preference
lightning.explanation: With two elements, mid equals lo, so nums[lo] == nums[mid]. The single-element 'half' is trivially sorted; strict < sends the search right and returns -1 for a target sitting at hi.

lightning.question: Follow-up: duplicates are now allowed (e.g. [2,2,2,3,2]). What happens to the worst case?
options: Degrades to O(n) — when nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] neither half is provably sorted, so you can only shrink the range by one
Still O(log n) with the same code
lightning.explanation: All-equal ends carry zero information about which side holds the target, so the only safe move is lo++ / hi-- — an adversarial input full of duplicates forces linear time.
